# Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures

Thomas Massoni∗ Jonathan Zung†

October 20, 2026

## Abstract

We study the geography of taut foliations on compact 3-manifolds with toroidal boundary components. The central object of our work is the set of boundary multislopes realized by foliations transverse to a fixed flow on such a manifold. We prove that these sets exhibit remarkable structural properties—rationality, rigidity, and convexity—which motivate the name ziggurats. Our main tool, of independent interest, is a two-way correspondence between foliations and contact structures on 3-manifolds with boundary: we generalize the Eliashberg–Thurston theorem, which produces pairs of positive and negative contact structures from foliations, and a construction of the first author, which builds foliations from such contact pairs. Using both directions of this correspondence, we bring contact-geometric methods to bear on the architecture of ziggurats.

## 0 Introduction

### 0.1 Motivation

A foliation F on a 3-manifold M is a decomposition of M into surfaces locally modeled on R2 × R. A foliation is taut if it admits a transverse loop through every point, or equivalently, if it admits a transverse nonwandering flow (see Definition 4.4). An outstanding problem in 3-manifold theory is to determine which 3-manifolds admit taut foliations.

Question 0.1. Given a nonwandering flow Φ on M, does there exist a (necessarily taut) foliation transverse to Φ?

A basic operation on 3-manifolds is that of Dehn surgery along knots or links. It allows one not only to create new manifolds from old ones, but also to study them in families; concretely, one may fix a link in a given 3-manifold and study all of its Dehn surgeries at the same time by varying the surgery slopes. This Dehn surgery perspective also permits us to focus on simpler flows on manifolds with boundary. For example, in the important cases where Φ is a periodic flow or a transitive pseudo-Anosov flow, any (M, Φ) arises from surgery along a collection of orbits of a suspension flow (see [Fri83; Bru95] for the pseudo-Anosov case). This motivates the following definition:

Definition 0.2. Let M be a compact oriented 3-manifold with n framed toroidal boundary components, and Φ be a nonwandering flow on M tangent to ∂M. We define

Z(Φ) :=  s | ∃foliation F transverse to Φ with well-defined boundary multislope s ⊂Rn.

We refer to Z(Φ) as the (foliation) ziggurat of Φ, borrowing the evocative terminology coined by Calegari–Walker for related sets arising in circle dynamics (see Section 0.3).

A complete understanding of Z(Φ) would essentially answer Question 0.1 on all Dehn fillings of (M, Φ). The goal of this article is to prove a variety of structural results for Z(Φ) which will explain the moniker “ziggurat”. Before stating our results, let us survey some examples in which Z(Φ) is well understood.

### 0.2 Ziggurats for periodic and pseudo-Anosov flows

A privileged role in the theory is played by periodic and pseudo-Anosov flows. A flow Φ without fixed points is periodic if there exists T > 0 such that ΦT is the identity. A flow is pseudo-Anosov if it is a hyperbolic flow with finitely many singular orbits modeled on semi-branched covers of standard hyperbolic orbits (p-prongs); see [Mos91; Mos92].

Conjecture 0.3 (Calegari, Thurston [Cal06; Thu97]). If F is a taut foliation on a closed atoroidal 3-manifold, then there exists a nonwandering flow Φ which is almost1 transverse to F and is either periodic or pseudo-Anosov.

This is a far-reaching generalization of Nielsen–Thurston theory for fibrations over S1. The flow should record how the conformal structures of leaves of F change in the transverse direction. Conjecture 0.3 is known in the Seifert fibered case by work of Thurston and Brittenham [Thu72; Bri93]. In the hyperbolic case, the theory of universal circles pioneered by Thurston in [Thu97] and extensively developed by Calegari, Dunfield, Fenley, and others has proven Conjecture 0.3 in many cases [CD03; Cal00; Fen05; Cal06]. In another line of work, Gabai–Mosher [Mos96; Gab97] and Landry–Tsang [LT25; LT26b] have resolved Conjecture 0.3 for finite depth foliations. Upcoming work of Landry–Taylor [LT26a] also proves uniqueness and finiteness results for pseudo-Anosov flows (almost-)transverse to a given finite depth taut foliation. In view of Conjecture 0.3, an ambitious yet principled route towards a classification of taut foliations on atoroidal 3-manifolds is first to classify the periodic and pseudo-Anosov flows on M, and then to answer Question 0.1 for each of them.

Periodic flows in dimension 3 are completely understood via the classification of Seifert fibered spaces. The foliation ziggurat Z(Φ) is also completely understood thanks to work of

Pseudo-Anosov flows, on the other hand, remain beyond the reach of a complete classification. Despite this, much progress has been made towards the following conjecture:

Conjecture 0.7. On any closed 3-manifold, there exist at most finitely many pseudo-Anosov flows up to orbit equivalence.

Gabai–Li [GL26] have recently announced a proof of Conjecture 0.7 for hyperbolic 3- manifolds, and Bowden–Colin have independently announced the Anosov case using different techniques [BC26]. Still, only a little is known about Z(Φ) in the pseudo-Anosov case. The first existence result was proven by Roberts:

Theorem 0.8 ([Rob01]). Suppose Φ is a pseudo-Anosov suspension flow on a fibration Σ◦ g →M →S1, where Σ◦ g is a genus g ≥1 surface with one boundary component. Then Z(Φ) contains an open interval around the slope of the fiber (the longitude).

Further progress has been made by Li–Roberts [LR14] who extended [Rob01] to arbitrary (nontrivial) knot complements in S3, Krishna [Kri20], Nie [Nie26], and Zhao [Zha26] who studied the maximal interval of slopes contained in Z(Φ) for some families of knots, and Santoro [San24] who extended the techniques to 2-bridge links. All of these results rely on [Li02] to produce taut foliations from a branched surface obtained from small modifications of a sutured hierarchy. Using the technology of veering triangulations [Ago11; Gué16], we began a systematic experimental exploration of Z(Φ) for many different pseudo-Anosov flows in [Zun24]. Our software is available online [Zun26]. Several examples of (approximations to) Z(Φ) are shown in Figure 3. These figures display intricate staircasing phenomena, especially near topologically significant multislopes. These experiments were our first hint that features of the Jankins–Neumann ziggurat might reappear in the setting of hyperbolic manifolds. We will explain many of these phenomena in this article.

### 0.3 Ziggurats in circle dynamics

Let f rot : ^ Homeo+(S1) →R be the (lifted) rotation number of a (lifted) circle homeomorphism. In [CW11], Calegari–Walker studied the extremal rotation number problem: Given a word w in the generators a, b, determine the set

Z(w) :=  (r, s, t) ∃a, b ∈ ^ Homeo+(S1) with f rot(a) = r, f rot(b) = s, f rot(w) = t  ⊂R3.

When w = ab, Z(w) is the Jankins–Neumann ziggurat up to a change of coordinates. They show that when w is an arbitrary positive word (i.e., it does not contain a−1 or b−1), many of the structural properties of the Jankins–Neumann ziggurat persist. In particular, they show that Z(w) is assembled from blocks with rational corners. Except for the Jankins–Neumann ziggurat, Z(w) does not appear to be a foliation ziggurat for any choice of Φ. Our methods are also quite different from [CW11]: Calegari–Walker rely on a combinatorial analysis of the interleaving pattern of the fixed point sets of a and b, while we rely heavily on 3-manifold technology including contact geometry. We think that there ought to be a more general framework which simultaneously generalizes [CW11] and the present work.

Question 0.9. What is the broadest dynamical context in which the ziggurat phenomenon occurs?

### 0.4 Foliations and contact structures

Eliashberg and Thurston showed in [ET98] that a cooriented C2-foliation without spherical leaves on a closed 3-manifold may be approximated by positive and negative contact structures. Bowden and Kazez–Roberts generalized this to C0-foliations [Bow16a; KR17]. More recently, the first author proved a converse, reconstructing a foliation from a suitable pair of contact structures [Mas24]. With these tools in hand, we can pass back and forth between the foliated and contact worlds.

In this article, we refine both directions of this correspondence in the case when M has boundary: we upgrade the forward direction to give control over ∂ξ−and ∂ξ+, and we upgrade the reverse direction to give control over ∂F. We need the tools of both foliation theory and contact geometry to prove our strongest results. Roughly speaking, the condition for a 2-plane field to be a contact structure is open. Thus, the contact perspective offers the flexibility needed to prove that Z(Φ) is open near certain points. On the other hand, the condition for a 2-plane field to be (tangent to) a foliation is closed. Therefore, the foliation perspective is useful for proving that Z(Φ) is closed near certain points.

### 0.5 Notation

For the reader’s convenience, we include a short list of notation that will be used throughout the article.

• M: compact, oriented, connected 3-manifold, with nonempty boundary unless otherwise stated. The boundary components are framed tori and are numbered ∂1M, . . . , ∂nM.

• Φ: smooth, nonsingular, nonwandering flow on M tangent to ∂M having boundary slope +∞on each component of ∂M. Note that Φ need not be a linear flow on ∂M, but must have a well-defined boundary slope.

• Z(Φ): real multislopes realized by a (necessarily taut) C0-foliation positively transverse to Φ. In this article, multislopes are oriented.

• Z±(Φ): real multislopes realized by positive/negative contact structures positively transverse to Φ.

• Zℵ(Φ): the set of generalized multislopes realized by C0-foliations positively transverse to Φ, where ℵis treated as a wildcard that can assume any real number.

• I := [0, 1].

### 0.7 Results

We establish two collections of results. First, we extend the approximation techniques of Eliashberg–Thurston and the construction of foliations from contact structures by the first author to the setting of manifolds with boundary. Second, we apply those results to the study of ziggurats. Our results relating foliations and contact structures might be of independent interest.

### 0.7.1 Foliations and contact structures on manifolds with boundary

We assume ∂M ̸= ∅. We say that the boundary foliation of a positive (resp. negative) contact structure dominates another foliation G on ∂M if it pointwise has higher (resp. lower) slope than G. See Figure 5.

Theorem A (Eliashberg–Thurston with boundary). Let F be a C0-foliation on M transverse to ∂M.

1. (Coarse version) Assume that (M, F) is not homeomorphic to either of the following:

• S1 × D2 with the standard foliation by disks,

• T2 × I with a foliation semiconjugate to an irrational foliation.

Then for every ε > 0, there exists a positive (resp. negative) contact structure ξ which is ε-close to TF in the C0 topology, and whose boundary foliation dominates a foliation G = Gε on ∂M which is monotone equivalent to ∂F.

2. (Fine version) If moreover F has neither compact planar leaves nor T2-type planar minimal sets (Definition 7.2), then G can be chosen isotopic to ∂F along ∂M.

Here, we say that two foliations are monotone equivalent if they can be connected by a finite sequence (zigzag) of semiconjugacies. We will prove a more precise version in the presence of compact planar leaves and T2-type planar minimal sets; see Theorem 8.24 below. Note that this theorem does not involve any transverse flow, as opposed to its converse.

Theorem B (Converse to Eliashberg–Thurston with boundary). Let (ξ−, ξ+) be a contact pair on M positively transverse to Φ. Furthermore, let G∂be a smooth foliation on ∂M which is transverse to Φ|∂M and which is dominated by ∂ξ−and ∂ξ+ along ∂M. Then, there exists a C0-foliation F on M transverse to Φ (and in particular to ∂M) such that ∂F is semiconjugate to G∂, via a map ∂F →G∂.

Here, a contact pair (ξ−, ξ+) is a pair of contact structures with opposite signs with respect to the orientation on M. The reader should imagine that the foliation G∂in the theorem is “sandwiched” between ξ−and ξ+ along ∂M, as in Figure 5a. Unfortunately, it might not be possible to make ∂F isotopic to G∂in general, but this result will be powerful enough for all our applications.

### 0.7.2 Applications to ziggurats

In the rest of the introduction and also in Part III, we make the following standing assumptions unless otherwise stated.

Standing Assumption 0.10.

• M is a compact, connected, oriented 3-manifold with toroidal boundary components. The boundary components of M are framed. We also assume that M ≇S1 × D2 and M ≇T2 × I, so that the hypotheses of the coarse Eliashberg–Thurston theorem (item 1 of Theorem A) are satisfied.

• Φ is a smooth, nonsingular and nonwandering flow on M whose restriction to each boundary component of ∂M induces a Reebless foliation of slope +∞(the degeneracy slope).

Notice that changing the framings on the boundaries of M without modifying the degeneracy slopes simply induces a translation in Rn by an integer vector.

The master result that will allow us to apply techniques from contact geometry to the study of ziggurats is the following ziggurat intersection theorem, which is a consequence of Theorems A and B.

Theorem C. The foliation ziggurat Z(Φ) is exactly the intersection of the negative and positive contact ziggurats: Z−(Φ) ∩Z+(Φ) = Z(Φ).

The next few results will be rather immediate applications of Theorem C. First, we show that the ziggurat Z(Φ) satisfies a strong convexity property.

Definition 0.11. A subset A ⊂Rn is box-convex if for all x, y ∈A satisfying x ≤y, we have [x, y] ⊂A.

Remark 0.12. Box-convexity is stable under taking intersections and under closure.

Definition 0.13. Let S ⊂Rn. The box-closure of S, denoted by [S], is defined as

[S] := n s ∈Rn | ∃s± ∈S, s−≤s ≤s+o .

It is the smallest box-convex subset of Rn containing S.

Theorem D (Box-convexity). The set Z(Φ) is box-convex.

When n = 1, i.e., when M has a unique boundary component, this result simply means that Z(Φ) ⊂R is an interval. When n ≥2, more complicated shapes can appear.

We next establish some properties of rational and irrational slopes.

Theorem E (Dehn filling). Suppose s ∈Qn. The multislope s is realized by a Φ-horizontal foliation with linear boundary type (foliation by circles) if and only if one of the following holds:

• s ∈int Z(Φ), or

• Φ is a suspension flow of a fibration with compact planar fibers with multislope s.

### 0.8 Further directions

Rigidity of extremal foliations. Given a circle bundle over a surface attaining the extremal value of the Euler number permitted by the Milnor–Wood inequality, Matsumoto proved that there is a unique horizontal foliation up to monotone equivalence [Mat87]. Does any similar rigidity property hold for foliations achieving extremal points of Z(Φ)?

Multiple pseudo-Anosov flows. Our results focus on foliations transverse to a single flow. In view of Conjecture 0.3 (for hyperbolic 3-manifolds), it is expected that one must consider all pseudo-Anosov flows simultaneously to complete the picture and survey the full geography of taut foliations on a given 3-manifold.

Note that rationality and the sphericity of slippery points would follow from the finiteness conjecture for pseudo-Anosov flows combined with the corresponding theorem for the individual ziggurats Z(Φi). As a first step towards this conjecture, it would be interesting to understand how the ziggurats for pseudo-Anosov flows coming from adjacent fibered faces of the Thurston norm ball fit together.

Heegaard Floer homology. There are many tantalizing conjectures relating Heegaard Floer homology and taut foliations, chief among which is the L-space conjecture [BGW13; Juh15]. It predicts that the existence of a taut coorientable foliation on an irreducible rational homology 3-sphere is equivalent to the nonvanishing of a certain flavor of Heegaard Floer homology. A step toward this conjecture would be to show that the space of non-L-space surgeries on a given link shares the same structural properties as the foliation ziggurats we study in this article. Let s be a relative spinc structure on M. Then s induces a spinc structure on every Dehn filling of M up to an ambiguity of multiples of the Poincaré duals of the Dehn surgery cores. Let ZHF (M, s) be the set of (rational) multislopes such that the corresponding Dehn filling is a non-L-space in at least one of the induced spinc structures.

### 0.9 Organization of the article

The article is divided into three main parts and three appendices.

• In Part I, we collect the preliminaries on foliations, contact structures, and flows needed in the rest of the article. While most of the results in Part I are not fundamentally new, we recommend reading Section 2 about foliations on T2 for our notation and conventions.

• In Part II, we prove our version of the Eliashberg–Thurston theorem and its converse for 3-manifolds with boundary (Theorem A and Theorem B). This is the technical heart of the article and can be used as a black box for the next part.

• In Part III, we give applications to the structure of the ziggurat Z(Φ) and prove Theorems C to N. Most of these applications are rather direct consequences of Part II, but this third part can be read without a detailed understanding of the proofs in Part II.

• In Appendix A, we prove a technical result on mean curvature flow on the 2-torus used in Section 2. In Appendix B, we study ziggurats in the special cases of disk and annulus suspensions, which are excluded from our main theorems. In Appendix C, we discuss a more general framework for describing “inadmissible” boundary foliations.

1 C0-foliations and laminations

A foliation is a decomposition of an n-manifold into k-dimensional submanifolds (leaves) locally topologically modeled on Rk × Rn−k. We are exclusively concerned with the cases (n, k) = (3, 2) (codimension 1 foliations on M) and (n, k) = (2, 1) (codimension 1 foliations on ∂M). In this article, a C0-foliation is a foliation with C1 leaves and a continuous tangent plane field. Every foliation is topologically isotopic to a C0-foliation (and even with smooth leaves) by [Cal01, Theorem 3.4]. In general, the foliations we consider on manifolds with boundary are transverse to the boundary. There are two natural topologies on the space of foliations. Two foliations are ε tangentially close if their tangent plane fields are ε-close. We call the induced topology the tangential topology. Two foliations F1 and F2 are ε-C0-close if for every point p ∈M and every 1-Lipschitz pointed C1 immersion f1 : (B1/ε, 0) →(M, p) with image contained in a leaf of F1, there is a pointed C1 immersion f2 : (B1/ε, 0) →(M, p) with image contained in a leaf of F2 which is ε-C1 close to f1, and similarly with F1 and F2 swapped. We call the induced topology the C0 topology. The tangential topology is coarser than the C0 topology, because there can be different foliations tangent to the same continuous plane field.

2 Foliations of T2

Foliations on T2 naturally arise in the boundary of foliations on 3-manifolds. In this section we establish terminology for describing foliations on T2 as well as some basic properties. While the results may appear technical, all of the rationality, stability, and flexibility results we prove for Z(Φ) have their roots in phenomena on T2.

### 2.1 Slope and type

When a leaf spirals to the right (resp. left) onto a closed curve, we say that the closed curve has ♯(resp. ♭) type spiraling. A sharp (♯) annulus is a C0-foliated S1 × [0, 1] with two compact leaves along the boundary, and whose remaining leaves are noncompact and spiral onto the compact leaves toward the right; see Figure 12a. Similarly, a flat (♭) annulus is a similar C0-foliated annulus, except that the noncompact leaves spiral onto the compact leaves toward the left; see Figure 12b. Finally, a Reeb annulus is one for which leaves spiral to the left onto S1 × {0} and to the right along S1 × {1} (or vice versa). A ♯, ♭, or Reeb lamination is a sublamination of the corresponding foliation with at least one noncompact leaf. Whenever λ is a closed leaf of a foliation of T2, one may blow up λ and insert a ♯or ♭ annulus. We call this operation a ♯or ♭blowup.

Lemma 2.18 (Instability of ♮or ♯-type foliations). Suppose G1 and G2 are two Reebless C0-foliations of T2 with finite slopes, and G1 has pointwise greater slope than G2. Then

## 3 Contact structures

In this section, we collect elementary facts about contact structures that will be useful later. We refer to [Etn03; Gei08; Mas14] for excellent introductions to contact geometry. A three-dimensional positive (resp. negative) contact structure, usually denoted ξ, is a cooriented 2-plane field on an oriented 3-manifold M which is “completely nonintegrable”. Concretely, it may be expressed as ker α for some smooth 1-form α satisfying α ∧dα > 0 (resp. α ∧dα < 0), where the sign involves the orientation on M. We make the following convention: for a negative contact structure, the correspondence between its orientation and coorientation is obtained from the orientation on M induced by the contact structure itself, namely, the opposite of the chosen orientation on M. Moreover, a flow or vector field is positively transverse to it if it is positively transverse with respect to its orientation and not its coorientation. In other words, a vector field X is positively transverse to a negative contact structure ξ−with contact form α−if α−(X) < 0. If ∂M ̸= ∅, we will typically require that ξ is transverse to ∂M. A contact structure ξ on M is overtwisted if there exists an embedded disk in int M which is transverse to ξ, except along its boundary and its center where they are tangent. Equivalently, there is a standard model for overtwisted disks, see for instance [Gei08, Example 2.1.6]. A contact structure that is not overtwisted is called tight. Importantly, the contact condition is open in the C1-topology, and contact structures are stable, in the sense of Gray stability: if (ξt)t∈[0,1] is a (smooth) path of contact structures which is constant near ∂M, then there exists an isotopy (ϕt)t∈[0,1] of M supported away from ∂M satisfying ϕ∗ t ξt = ξ0 for all t ∈[0, 1]. However, the situation is more complicated when we allow modifications at the boundary. By Darboux’s theorem, every (positive) contact structure is locally of the form ker �dz + xdy . For the purpose of studying foliations, we will consider pairs of contact structures with opposite signs. The relationship between foliations and contact pairs was originally studied in [CF11] and the theory was further developed by the first author in [Mas24], in the setting of closed manifolds. A positive contact pair on M is a pair of (cooriented) contact structures (ξ−, ξ+) such that ξ−and ξ+ have no negative tangencies, or equivalently, if there is a smooth vector field positively transverse to both contact structures. When ∂M ̸= ∅, we say that (ξ−, ξ+) is adapted to the boundary if ∂ξ+ is positively transverse to ∂ξ−(see Figure 4). A contact pair (ξ−, ξ+) is taut (“fortement tendue” in [CF11]) if for every point p ∈M, there exists a closed loop positively transverse to both ξ−and ξ+ and passing through p. See [Mas24] for other characterizations of tautness, which also hold for manifolds with boundary. Moreover, we have:

Lemma 3.4. If (ξ−, ξ+) is a taut contact pair on a closed 3-manifold, then ξ−and ξ+ are both universally tight.

A proof is sketched in [CH20, Section 5], see also [Mas24, Proposition 3.2].

## 4 Flows

In this article, a flow is an R-action on M without stationary points whose orbits are C1 and tangent to a nowhere vanishing C0 vector field. In particular, flows are tangent to ∂M.

### 4.1 Blowup and blowdown

Definition 4.1. Let Φ be a smooth flow on a compact 3-manifold M. A blowup of (M, Φ) along a closed orbit γ ⊂intM of Φ is a pair (M◦, Φ◦), where M◦is a compact 3-manifold with torus boundary and Φ◦is a flow on M◦tangent to the boundary, together with a map π : M◦→M such that

1. There exist smooth local coordinates (r, θ, ϕ) around ∂M◦(where r parametrizes the normal direction, ϕ parametrizes the longitudinal direction, θ parametrizes the meridional direction) and cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, ϕ) in a neighborhood of γ (where γ lies along {r = 0}), such that π has the form

π(r, θ, ϕ) = (f(r), θ, ϕ)

for some smooth increasing function f : [0, 1] →[0, 1] satisfying f(0) = 0. In particular, π sends ∂M◦to γ, collapsing leaves of a linear foliation on ∂M◦to points.

### 4.2 Nonwandering flows

Ultimately, we are interested in pseudo-Anosov flows and periodic flows. However, we prove many of our results for the larger class of nonwandering flows. For some results, we will impose additional conditions that are automatically satisfied for suitable pseudo-Anosov and periodic flows.

Definition 4.4. Let Φ = (φt) be a (topological) flow on M. We say that Φ is a nonwandering flow if for every nonempty open set U ⊂M and every T > 0, there exists t ≥T such that φt(U) ∩U ̸= ∅.

The following classes of flows are nonwandering:

• Topologically transitive flows,

• Volume preserving flows (by the Poincaré recurrence theorem),

• Flows whose orbits are all periodic.

Importantly, nonwandering flows are “witnesses” of tautness. Indeed, any (everywhere) taut foliation or taut contact pair admits a transverse volume preserving flow, which is in particular nonwandering. Conversely, we have:

Lemma 4.5. Let Φ = (φt) be a nonwandering flow on M tangent to a continuous nonvanishing vector field X.

2. Any contact pair (positively) transverse to Φ is taut.

Given a point p ∈M, we would like to construct a C-positive curve (i.e., a curve whose derivative lies in C) which passes through p. Reparametrize the flow to move at unit speed. A flow Φ is periodic if it has no fixed points, and there exists T > 0 such that ΦT is the identity.6 Periodic flows are linear on ∂M, so they satisfy Zℵ(Φ) = Z(Φ). Periodic flows do not in general satisfy condition BSF, but they satisfy the following weaker condition:

Definition 4.6. A flow Φ is locally branched surface finite (LBSF) if for every p ∈Rn, there is a neighborhood U of p and a finite collection of Φ-horizontal branched surfaces Σ1, . . . , Σm such that, up to the action of flow preserving homeomorphisms of (M, Φ) rel boundary, every Φ-horizontal foliation with generalized boundary multislope in U is carried by some Σi. Here, a generalized boundary multislope is in U if some substitution of its ℵ components with real numbers lies in U.

### 4.4 Pseudo-Anosov flows

A pseudo-Anosov flow is a flow on a 3-manifold locally modeled on the suspension flow of a pseudo-Anosov surface homeomorphism. ## 7 Typology of minimal sets

In this section, we analyze and classify all the possible types of minimal sets for a cooriented C0-foliation on M transverse to ∂M. To that end, it is convenient to classify the topological types of laminations on M which are transverse to ∂M. Each boundary component of a leaf of a lamination transverse to ∂M is either open (homeomorphic to R) or closed (homeomorphic to S1). Each open boundary component may lie in a boundary component of ∂M with irrational slope, or it may spiral on both sides towards two closed curves bounding an annulus (or a single curve bounding a “degenerate annulus”) on a boundary component of M, in the fashion of a ♯, ♭, or Reeb annulus. 3. λ becomes homeomorphic to R2 after filling the closed boundary components with disks and deleting the open boundary components. In that case, π1(λ) is freely generated by its closed boundary components.

## Part II From foliations to contact structures and back

In [ET98], Eliashberg and Thurston proved that any C2-foliation different from the fibration by spheres on S1 × S2 on a closed manifold can be approximated by positive and negative contact structures. This result has been extended to C0-foliations by Bowden [Bow16a] and independently Kazez–Roberts [KR17]. In [Mas24], the first author proved a converse result on the construction of C0-foliations from suitable contact pairs, still in the setting of closed manifolds. The goal of this part is to extend these theorems to manifolds with toroidal boundary. In the case of the Eliashberg–Thurston approximation theorem, we will carefully keep track of how the boundary foliation is modified; this is perhaps the most difficult result of this article. The converse theorem for manifolds with boundary will be reduced to the closed manifold case by an elementary reflection trick.

## 8 Eliashberg–Thurston with boundary

As before, we assume that M is a connected, compact, oriented 3-manifold with nonempty boundary ∂M ̸= ∅. Let F be a cooriented C0-foliation on M which is transverse to ∂M. Our goal is to approximate F by positive and negative contact structures ξ± with precise control over the characteristic foliations of ξ± along ∂M. In particular, if ∂M is framed and F realizes a multislope s along ∂M, we would like to construct contact approximations realizing the same multislope s along ∂M. We refer to this version of the Eliashberg–Thurston theorem with boundary as the coarse version. It applies to any foliation F as above which is not homeomorphic to the standard foliation by disks on S1 × D2, or to a blowup of an irrational foliation on T2 × I. This coarse version does not allow one to control the boundary type of the contact approximations along ∂M. For some applications, we will need a more precise result which will allow us to improve the boundary type of the foliation (e.g., turn a ♯boundary foliation into one with strictly higher slope), provided that certain obstructions (compact genus 0 surfaces and T2-type planar minimal sets, see below) do not appear. We will refer to this version as the fine version of the Eliashberg–Thurston theorem with boundary. In particular, this will allow us to remove certain ♭, ♯, ♮, and Reeb regions appearing in ∂F in the unobstructed setting.

Remark 8.1. After some minor adjustments near ∂M, one can double the foliation F on the doubled manifold M = M ∪∂M (−M), and apply the standard version of Eliashberg–Thurston theorem (for C0-foliations) to the closed manifold M, provided that F is not homeomorphic to the standard foliation by disks on S1 × D2 (which would yield the standard foliation by spheres on S1 × S2). This way, one obtains positive and negative contact approximations to F on M. However, this strategy provides no control over characteristic foliations of the

contact structures along ∂M, beyond C0-closeness. This is even more problematic when the original foliation is only C0, as the boundary slope may be modified in a dramatic way.

We now give a rough overview of the proof strategy for the coarse and fine versions. While the fine version essentially follows the same steps, it will require a much more careful analysis of various key ingredients; in particular, T3-type planar minimal sets will be handled separately using new techniques.

• Step 1. First, we make compact leaves isolated by performing suitable blowdowns and blowups. The new boundary foliation is monotone-equivalent to the original one. In the absence of compact genus 0 leaves, we can arrange that the new boundary foliation is obtained by blowdowns and trivial blowups, which is relevant to the fine version. This step is very similar to Step 1 from [Bow16a, Section 8].

• Step 2. Then, we perform blowups near the (finitely many) minimal sets to create suitable holonomy there, as in Step 2 of [Bow16a, Section 8]. While the boundary foliation is only modified by some monotone-equivalence, more care is needed to prevent nontrivial blowups for the fine version, in the absence of compact genus 0 leaves. Besides, T3-type planar minimal sets will be treated separately using a rather hands on strategy.

• Step 3. We proceed as in [Bow16a, Lemma 4.1] to create nice annular fences near holonomy curves. For the fine version we also create “toroidal holes” by drilling out neighborhoods of some transverse closed curves in order to handle the T3-type planar minimal sets. We further consider suitable “boundary windows” along ∂M (including on the newly created toroidal boundary components). We then remove neighborhoods of the annular fences to obtain a certain type of manifold with boundary and concave corners that we call manifolds with (annular boundary) fences and (boundary) windows. Crucially, we will arrange that every point in the resulting manifold can be connected to a boundary fence or window by a smooth curve tangent to the foliation.

• Step 4. Adapting techniques developed in [Bow16a], we modify the foliation along ribbons connecting fences and windows to the “genuine” boundary components and improve the boundary foliation along the latter, at the expense of also modifying the foliation along the boundary fences and windows. The reader should think of the fences and windows as “drains” which absorb the modifications at the genuine boundary along the ribbons.

• Step 5. We can now apply a suitable version of the main result of [Bow16a] to approximate the foliation and obtain a contact structure which dominates the boundary foliation obtained from Step 4 along the genuine boundary components (after possibly making it slightly worse inside of the windows).

• Step 6. Finally, we extend the approximating contact structures by filling the annular fences as in [Bow16a, Lemma 5.6]. We also fill the toroidal boundary components corresponding to the T3-type planar minimal sets using the results in Section 8.3.4 below.

We then use variations of smoothing ribbons from [Bow16a] to “twist” the foliation along the ribbons and transport modifications of the genuine boundary components to those drilled regions and to the windows. This will allow us to make the boundary foliation “better” than the original one, except inside the windows where it will become slightly “worse”. These modifications will take place on what we call manifolds with fences and windows.

### 8.2 Coarse version

In this section, we adapt the strategy of Bowden [Bow16a] to the case of manifolds with boundary and prove:

Theorem 8.12 (Coarse Eliashberg–Thurston with boundary). Let F be a cooriented C0- foliation on M transverse to ∂M. Assume that F is neither homeomorphic to the standard foliation by disks on S1 × D2, nor to a foliation on T2 × I semiconjugate to an irrational foliation. Then for every ε > 0, there exists a positive (resp. negative) contact structure which is ε-C0-close to TF and which dominates a 1-dimensional C0-foliation G on ∂M which is monotone equivalent to ∂F.

In this theorem, the contact approximations might not dominate ∂F itself, but they dominate a foliation G on ∂M obtained from ∂F by small Denjoy blowups and blowdowns, and C0-small isotopies. Notice that G depends on ε a priori. Nevertheless, this readily implies:

Corollary 8.13 (Boundary multislope). Under the hypothesis of Theorem 8.12, if F has a well-defined boundary multislope s, then it is approximated by positive and negative contact structures realizing the same boundary multislope s.

As mentioned before, this coarse version does not allow us to control the precise boundary types of the contact approximations, only their multislopes. However, this is enough for most of our applications.

We note that the hypotheses on F in Theorem 8.12 are necessary for the purpose of approximating foliations with contact structures:

Lemma 8.14. 1. The standard foliation by disks on S1 × D2 cannot be C0-approximated by contact structures with boundary slope 0 for the standard boundary framing.

2. A linear irrational foliation F on T2×I cannot be C0-approximated by contact structures realizing the same boundary slopes as F.

Proof. We first argue that there is no contact structure on S1 × D2 transverse to the S1- direction and with slope 0 along ∂(S1 × D2). Indeed, such a contact structure would have a closed characteristic along ∂(S1 × D2) which would be a Legendrian curve bounding an embedded disk, implying that it is overtwisted. However, a horizontal contact structure on S1 × D2 is necessarily tight, see for instance [Vog16, Theorem 2.27]. More generally, if F is a C1-foliation by disks on S1 × D2, then there exists a smooth diffeomorphism φ : S1 × D2 →S1 × D2 such that φ(F) is transverse to the S1-direction. Indeed, there exists a C1 diffeomorphism sending F to the standard foliation by disks, and any smoothing of it satisfies the desired conditions.9

To prove the second item, we may assume that F is a product G × I, where G is an irrational foliation on T2 = S1 × S1. In particular, it is transverse to the first S1 factor. We now assume by contradiction that such an approximating contact structure exists. Then, “trimming” the boundary yields a contact structure ξ with strictly better boundary slopes, which we can arrange to be rational and realized by linear characteristic foliations. Then,

Following [Bow16a], we consider the leaves near L0 intersecting a neighborhood of γ. If the curves parallel to γ in those leaves are all leafwise homotopically trivial, we claim that L0 is either a torus or a cylinder. Indeed, we may consider the doubling of F along ∂M, together with (a connected component of) the doubling bL0 of L0 whose nearby leaves satisfy a similar property. • Blowdowns and blowups of type ♮/♯(resp. ♮/♭) away from the boundaries of the aforementioned minimal sets,

Under the hypothesis of the corollary, if F has a well-defined boundary type, then it can approximated by (positive and negative) contact structures with the same boundary type, as in the second item of Theorem A.

In general, unstable compact planar leaves and T2-type planar minimal sets constitute obstructions to finding dominating contact structures for ∂F, up to isotopy, since we might not be able to add attracting holonomy near them, see Lemma 8.28 below. A mitosis of L is a C0-small modification of F obtained as follows: we blow up L and add canceling holonomies around γ1 and γ2, which creates a product region L × [0, ε] with parallel boundaries L × {0} and eL = L × {ε}. We can further arrange that all the leaves between L and eL are noncompact and accumulate on both L and eL. In particular, eL is the only new minimal set produced by the blowup. Notice that we only create trivial Denjoy blowups along γ3, . . . , γℓ, and that we have some freedom in choosing the holonomies around γ1 and γ2. For instance, we can make one ♯and the other ♭, or vice versa. This operation is useful for preparing for the application of Theorem 8.24 while maintaining control over the coarse slopes of γ1 and γ2 and on the fine slopes of γ3, . . . , γℓ. Indeed, the new leaf eL has two special boundary components eγ1 and eγ2, parallel to γ1 and γ2, respectively. We declare γ1 to be a distinguished boundary component of L, and eγ2 to be a distinguished boundary component of eL. Then, performing ♭/♯modifications on γ1 and eγ2 (independently of each other) do not change the slopes on ∂iM and ∂jM, since each of these curves have a parallel, unmodified curve of the same slope, namely, eγ1 and γ2. A Mean curvature flow for foliations on T2

Mean curvature flow or curve shortening flow is a geometric flow for curves on Riemannian surfaces. Given an initial curve γ0 : [0, 1] →S, the curve evolves by

dγt(x)

dt = κ⃗n,

where κ is the curvature and ⃗n is the unit normal pointing toward the convex side of γ. This partial differential equation can be considered as gradient flow for the length functional on γ; hence it tends to simplify curves. Indeed a series of work by Gage, Hamilton, Grayson, and others culminating in [Gra89] proves that mean curvature flow on a closed curve in a Riemannian surface either shrinks to a point or converges to a closed geodesic [Gag90; GH86; Gra87]. A key property of mean curvature flow is the avoidance principle, which states that mean curvature flow applied to a pair of curves does not create new intersections. In particular, an embedded curve remains embedded during mean curvature flow. We consider leafwise mean curvature flow (LMCF): a geometric flow on foliations under which each leaf evolves by standard mean curvature flow. Thanks to the avoidance principle, this flow (as long as it is defined) preserves the property of being a foliation. Taking the interval (r, s) arbitrarily small gives the desired convergence.

Lemma B.4. Taut foliations on S1 × D2 and T2 × I transverse to the boundary are classified as follows:

1. If F is a taut C0-foliation on S1 × D2 transverse to the boundary, then F is isotopic to the standard foliation by disks.

2. If F is a taut C0-foliation on T2 × I transverse to the boundary, then F is isotopic to a product of a foliation on T2 with I.

Proof. We prove each item in turn.

1. First, suppose ∂F contains a curve γ of slope 0. Since leaves of taut foliations are π1-injective, γ bounds a disk in a leaf of F. Now the Reeb stability theorem implies that F is a foliation by disks and hence is standard.

Now suppose that ∂F does not contain a closed curve of slope 0. We will find a null-homotopic transversal to F, which will contradict tautness of F. If ∂F is Reebless and has slope ̸= 0, then we can find the null-homotopic transversal in ∂F. If ∂F has a Reeb component, we may choose a leaf λ of F containing a closed curve on ∂M. Since this closed curve does not have slope 0 by assumption, π1(λ) is nontrivial. After lifting to a finite cover, we may assume that π1(λ) surjects onto π1(S1 × D2). Leaves of taut foliations are π1-injective, so we know π1(λ) ∼= Z. If λ is compact, then it most be an annulus, and therefore must separate M, contradicting tautness of F. If λ is noncompact, then it accumulates on itself. Choose a short transversal from λ to itself, and close it up to a positively monotone curve γ using an arc in λ. Since π1(λ) surjects onto π1(M), we choose the closure so that γ is null-homotopic. After a small isotopy, we get a closed null-homotopic (topological) transversal, contradicting tautness.

2. That Z(Φ) is contained in the locus of homological longitudes follows from the classification in Lemma B.4. We need to show that Z(Φ) is convex. Given any two Φ-horizontal foliations F0 and F1, Lemma B.4 says that F0 and F1 are products of foliations G0 and G1 on T2 with an interval. Since Φ is nonwandering, F0 and F1 are taut and G0, G1 cannot have Reeb annuli. Therefore, F0 and F1 have measured sublaminations Λ0 and Λ1 realizing the boundary slopes of F0 and F1 respectively. Convex combinations Λt := (1 −t)Λ0 + tΛ1 for 0 ≤t ≤1 are horizontal measured laminations realizing boundary slopes which are convex combinations of s(∂F0) and s(∂F1). We need to show that all of these complete to Φ-horizontal foliations. Focus on one of the guts G of Λt, which is naturally a sutured manifold with horizontal boundary R+ ⊔R−. We can choose the vertical boundary of G to be tangent to Φ, so Φ enters along R−and exits along R+. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there exists an orbit of Φ which do not exit G. Compactness yields a small ball to which Φ recurs infinitely many times. Closing up the recurring flow lines of Φ, we obtain loops which homologically pair to zero with Λt (since they are disjoint from Λt) and pair non-negatively with Λ0 and Λ1 (since Φ is transverse to F0 and F1). It follows that they pair to zero with both Λ0 and Λ1. Then either s(∂F0) = s(∂F1) and we are done, or these recurring loops are contractible which contradicts tautness of F0 and F1. Thus, we can assume that every orbit of Φ passes from R−to R+. This implies that G is a product so that Λt can be completed to a Φ-horizontal foliation. This concludes our proof of convexity of Z(Φ).

To show that Z(Φ) has nontrivial interior, we may twist the transverse foliation by annuli along a ribbon connecting the two boundary components; the details are left to the reader.

## C To ℵand beyond

It is natural to consider foliations with boundary slope ±∞, or non-ℵtype foliations with Reeb annuli. For simplicity, we avoided addressing these foliations in the body of the article. C.2 Speculations and conjectures

We now propose some conjectures for ziggurats of generalized fine multislopes.

Conjecture C.7. The subsets Z± fine(Φ) ⊂S n are open.

Conjecture C.8. The posets Z± fine(Φ) are downwards and upwards closed, respectively.

These two conjectures would follow from the twisting and trimming trick, as well as from definition of the order and the topology on S .

We also conjecture that the following generalization of Theorem C holds, at least away from certain obstructed multislopes:

Conjecture C.9. If Φ admits no horizontal compact planar surfaces nor T2-type planar laminations, then Zfine(Φ) = Z− fine(Φ) ∩Z+ fine(Φ).

More generally, the equality holds away from obstructed multislopes.

Conjecture C.10 (Generalized closedness). If Φ is LBSF, then Zℵ,fine(Φ) is closed. Moreover, if Φ is ℵ-unobstructed, then

Zfine(Φ) = Zℵ,fine(Φ).

If Φ admits no horizontal compact planar surfaces nor T2-type planar laminations, then Zfine(Φ) is closed.

One could show that along the faces of Z(Φ), the multislopes are realized by foliations with ♭/♯boundary types along the boundaries corresponding to extremal coordinates (up to ℵ-degeneration). Therefore, those correspond to special subsets of Zfine(Φ). It would be interesting to describe those more precisely.

It remains to understand how to characterize slippery points in the context of generalized fine multislopes. As a first step, we propose a purely set-theoretic problem:

Conjecture C.11. If A ⊂S n is open and closed, then its projection to Rn is terraced.

Question C.12. What is the correct extension of the notion of slipperiness to Zfine(Φ), in terms of extremality with respect to ≺? In particular, how to characterize the slippery points “at infinity”?
